role: Quick statistics tool for bwx12 csv files: per-interval totals, statistics per kernel.
purpose: The script reads the csv files that the runner bwx12 wrote into one or more result folders. It computes the rate of each timed interval as the sum of the per-thread rates, and it prints per kernel the number of intervals and the lowest, the median and the highest rate.

main_flow.step: Split the arguments into flags (`--json`, `--pool`) and folders.
For each folder, `interval_rows` reads every `*.csv` file in the order of the file names with `read_csv`.
`read_csv` keeps per T row the CPU, the rate `bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9` and the flag. Per I row it keeps the printed `aggregate_GBps`.
`interval_rows` builds one row per interval (round, position, kernel): `total` = the sum of the thread rates, the same sum per mesh, `I_agg`, and the test `is_64_56`.
`summarize` groups the 64+56 rows by kernel and computes `n`, `min`, `median` and `max` of `total`. It runs once per folder, and once more over all folders with `--pool`.
Print Part 1 (one line per interval) and Part 2 (one line per kernel) as text, or print everything as JSON with numbers rounded to 3 decimals.

behavior_notes: Rate formula: `total` of an interval = the sum over its T rows of `bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9`, in GB/s (GB = 1e9 bytes). The bytes of each thread are divided by the elapsed time of that same thread. `elapsed_s` is the time from the clock read of the thread before its first timed kernel call to its last clock read of the interval. bwx12 prints it with 6 decimals [Ref1] [Ref2].

This is not the formula of the I row. There bwx12 prints `aggregate_GBps` = the bytes of all threads divided by the longest elapsed time of one thread [Ref1]. The script shows that value as `I_agg` and does not use it in the statistics. In the 74 intervals of the 9 bwx12 folders of the rerun (parts L and C, control I), `total` is 0.00 to 0.02 GB/s above `I_agg` [Ref4].

stat_k120.py, the tool for part A, reports the `aggregate_GBps` that bandwidth.c prints. That value follows the formula of the I row. So a rate of part A and a rate of part L or part C come from two different formulas.

Rows used: T rows (thread rates), I rows (`I_agg` only) and `#` lines (`min_ms`, `stop` and `thp`, shown only). Of a T row the script reads the fields `round`, `pos`, `kernel`, `cpu`, `bytes`, `elapsed_s` and `flags`. It does not read `tid` (the number of the thread), `t_sched_s`, `t_start_s` and `t_end_s` (the common start time, the start time and the end time of the thread) or `passes` (the bytes of the thread divided by the bytes of one buffer pass). Of an I row it reads `round`, `pos`, `kernel` and `aggregate_GBps`. Rows not used: P rows and C rows.
Part 2 leaves out every interval that is not 64+56. In the 9 bwx12 folders of the rerun all 74 intervals are 64+56, so none is left out [Ref4].
A T row with the flag `late` stays in `total`. The script only counts it in the column `flg`. In the 9 bwx12 folders of the rerun no T row carries a flag [Ref4].

Part 2 groups by the kernel name only. It does not keep rounds, positions or files apart. A pool over folders with different kernel orders (`cfwd.csv` and `crev.csv` of part C) therefore mixes intervals that ran after different kernels [Ref3].

The old read kernel is the row `oldread`. The new read kernel is the row `read`. Of the three bwx12 parts of the rerun (part L, part C and control I), only part C runs the kernel `read` [Ref3]. The script does not compute a difference between kernels.

The script identifies an interval by round, position and kernel inside one csv file. If a file held two processes with the same kernel sequence, their T rows would form one interval with twice the threads, and the 64+56 test would reject it. Each csv file of the rerun holds one process [Ref3]. Each bwx12 folder of the rerun holds one csv file. So a Part 2 row of one folder is computed from 2 intervals of one process: round 0 and round 1 of the kernel [Ref4].

Rounding: all sums and statistics use the unrounded thread rates. The text report prints `total`, `I_agg`, the statistics and the rates of single threads with 2 decimals. It prints the sum per mesh with 1 decimal. The JSON output rounds every number to 3 decimals.

Role in the final numbers: for the bwx runners the facts sheet and the report page use the same formula as `total` [Ref6]. build_facts.py computes it with the parser of facts_data.py. It compares the intervals of 26 csv files from 20 folders with the output of `interval_rows` [Ref5]. These are the 9 csv files of the 9 bwx12 folders of the rerun and 17 csv files from 11 earlier folders of the runners bwx12 and bwx11. The 11 earlier folders hold 52 csv files, and the check does not compare the other 35. The facts sheet records this check as passed for 297 intervals, among them the 74 bwx12 intervals of the rerun [Ref6]. The check does not cover the csv files of the runner bwx [Ref5]. build_facts.py calls no other function of this file.

words.def: the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
the part L line, started from an idle machine, twice. It was added after the first numbers were seen. It is not part of the plan fixed before the run.
the read test of 2026-11-17 with 120 threads, run after the memory speed was lowered to 7200 MT/s (million transfers per second). Its parts are part A, part L, part C and control I.
1 GB is 1e9 bytes. Every rate is in GB/s.

the row kinds of a bwx csv file: one I row per interval, one T row per thread and interval, one P row per thread before the first interval and after each interval (it holds the page state of the buffer), and one C row per thread and interval with counter values.
the output of one bwx12 process. rx.sh (the script that starts bwx12) writes it into the result folder as `a6456.csv` (part L, control I), `cfwd.csv` or `crev.csv` (part C).
the rate of an interval in this tool: the sum over the threads of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9, in GB/s.
the field `aggregate_GBps` of the I row: the bytes of all threads divided by the longest elapsed time of one thread. bwx12 computes and prints it.
field 8 of a T row: the time from the clock read of the thread before its first timed kernel call to its clock read after the last one, in seconds [Ref2].
the flag that bwx12 writes into a T row when the thread started more than 100 us after the common start time.

three values of the header lines of a bwx csv file. `min_ms` is the length of a timed interval in ms that the command line asked for (6000 in the rerun). `stop` is the stop rule (`common` in the rerun). `thp=madvise` means that bwx12 asked Linux for transparent huge pages (2 MiB pages) for the buffers.
the stop rule used with bwx12 here: all threads stop at the same time (after 6 s).
the intervals of several folders taken together as one group.
the middle value of a sorted list. For an even number of values Python takes the mean of the two middle values.
the facts sheet is the file FACTS.md with its data file facts.json. It is the detailed record of the rerun. build_facts.py writes both from the raw result files and uses the parsers of facts_data.py.
the file `whole-chip-rerun-7200.html`. The script make_report.py writes it from facts.json.

functions.name: half
functions.what: Returns 0 for a CPU number below 64 (mesh 0) and 1 for every other CPU number (mesh 1).

functions.name: read_csv
functions.what: Parses one bwx csv file: header values, per-thread rate `bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9`, and the printed `aggregate_GBps` of each I row.

functions.name: interval_rows
functions.what: Builds one row per interval of a folder: `total` (sum of thread rates), sums per mesh, `I_agg`, flagged count, and the 64+56 test.

functions.name: summarize
functions.what: Per kernel over the 64+56 intervals: n, min, median and max of `total`, and the totals in file order.

functions.name: rounded
functions.what: Rounds every floating-point number inside a value to 3 decimals, for the JSON output.

functions.name: fmt_half
functions.what: Formats one mesh column of a Part 1 line.

functions.name: print_summary
functions.what: Prints the Part 2 table: one line per kernel.

functions.name: main
functions.what: Parses flags and folders, builds rows and statistics per folder and pooled, prints text or JSON.

Lines 3077 to 3084: the I row (`aggregate_GBps` = total bytes / longest elapsed time) and the T row (`elapsed_s` = end minus start of the thread, 6 decimals. Flag `late` or `-`).

line 1688: the clock read before the first timed kernel call. Lines 1690 to 1701: with the common stop the thread reads the clock after each chunk of 2 MiB and stops at the first read that is not before the common deadline. Lines 1722 to 1725: start time, end time and the `late` flag (line 133: more than 100000 ns after the common start).
